A 44-year-old Caucasian male was admitted to the emergency department after being trapped under the transmission system of a vehicle for an unknown amount of time, causing trauma to his chest and lungs. On admission, the patient had gasping breath, palpable regular pulses, and low blood pressure. He was urgently intubated and put on controlled mechanical ventilation due to his altered consciousness and respiratory distress. Upon examination, the patient's chest and upper body were congested, edematous, and covered with petechiae. Bilateral pneumothorax was detected, and bloody fluid was drained from his lungs through the endotracheal tube. The patient's condition improved after bilateral thoracostomies were inserted, draining air and blood. Arterial blood gases showed a pH of 7.246 and high levels of enzymes associated with muscle breakdown. A CT scan revealed mild brain edema and bilateral hemopneumothorax with lung contusions.

The patient was transferred to the ICU, where he was ventilated with volume-control mode, with a gas mixture that was quickly tapered to a fraction of inspired oxygen of 40%. Care was taken to prevent renal complications from potential traumatic rhabdomyolysis, and special attention was given to the brain edema with mannitol administration and frequent neurologic assessments. The patient improved quickly and was extubated on the second day of hospitalization, but remained disoriented and agitated until the fourth day. His facial and thoracic petechiae gradually faded within the next three days. The patient's enzymes returned to normal levels on the seventh day, and he was transferred to the thoracic surgical ward.

Recommendations:

The patient is advised to continue with follow-up appointments with his healthcare provider to monitor his progress. He should avoid activities that may place excessive stress on his chest and lungs, and he should report any changes in his symptoms to his healthcare provider immediately. The patient should also continue to take any medications as prescribed and follow a healthy lifestyle to aid in his recovery. 

For further medical attention, the patient is advised to contact the healthcare provider immediately should he experience any of the following symptoms: chest pain, shortness of breath, difficulty breathing, fever, or cough with abnormal sputum production.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission:
A 43-year-old male with primary hypothyroidism was admitted for evaluation of progressive fatigue, weakness, muscle and joint pain in the setting of recurrent fractures.

History of Present Illness:
The patient had been experiencing musculoskeletal pain in several locations including bilateral knees, ankles, left shoulder, left arm, and lower back which affected his overall functional status. He struggled to climb a flight of stairs, often grabbing the railing to pull himself up. A nuclear medicine bone scan showed abnormal uptake in bilateral ribs, vertebrae, right knee, hips, ankles, and feet. A lower extremity MRI showed stress fractures in left fibula, fifth metatarsal, and right tibia.

Course in Hospital:
The patient was started on calcitriol and phosphate supplements which significantly improved muscle weakness. Due to concern for TIO, a positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scan with 68Gallium (68Ga)-DOTATATE was performed which showed multiple lytic osseous lesions with increased somatostatin positive uptake seen throughout pelvis, ribs, ankles, and feet. However, after re-review with radiology, multiple areas of increased uptake were considered to be secondary to fractures, and left posterior acetabular lesion was presumed to be the tumor of interest given a remarkably higher standard uptake values (SUVmax) in this lesion compared to other lesions (SUVmax 20 vs. 4–5).

Procedure:
The left acetabular lesion was biopsied and pathology demonstrated a 1.4 cm phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor of the left acetabulum with uninvolved margins. The patient underwent radical resection of the tumor of the posterior left acetabulum with reconstruction of the posterior wall and posterior column of the acetabulum through a Kocher-Langenbach approach. His hip joint was able to be spared utilizing a 3D-printed custom bone cutting guide (CG) and intra-operative O-arm guided surgical navigation (Medtronic© Stealth) utilizing a navigated Sonopet Ultrasonic Bone Cutting Bovie (Stryker). The posterior wall and column of his acetabulum were constructed with a tantalum augment (Zimmer) and a pelvic reconstruction plate and screw construct (Synthes) after tumor removal.

Discharge Summary:
The patient was discharged with normal phosphorus and FGF23 levels, pain-free left hip, no evidence of hardware complication, back to hiking, and walking on the treadmill. Clinical and radiographic follow-up at 6 months postoperatively found him to be pain-free in his left hip, with almost complete resolution of bone pain, and no recurrence of fractures. Phosphorus level also remained normal at 3.4 mg/dL 6 months after surgery.

Admission:

History of Present Illness:
The patient had muscle and joint pain in both knees, ankles, left shoulder, left arm, and lower back.
This pain made it hard for him to climb stairs, so he often held the railing to pull himself up.
A bone scan showed abnormal activity in both ribs, spine, right knee, hips, ankles, and feet.
An MRI of his legs showed stress fractures in the left fibula, fifth toe bone, and right tibia.
Course in Hospital:
He was given vitamin D and phosphate supplements, which greatly improved his muscle weakness and overall strength.
Because doctors worried about a rare bone condition, they did a PET/CT scan with a special tracer.
The scan showed many bone areas with increased activity throughout the pelvis, ribs, ankles, and feet.
After reviewing the images with radiology, most of the increased activity was thought to be due to fractures.
The left hip lesion appeared to be the tumor, with a higher tracer value than other spots.
Procedure:
Doctors took a biopsy of the left hip lesion and found a 1.4-centimeter phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor.
The tumor was located in the left hip socket and had clean edges, meaning it was not invasive.
He had surgery to remove the tumor from the back of the left hip socket.
The surgery rebuilt the back wall and column of the hip socket using a special approach.
A 3D-printed bone guide and intraoperative navigation helped cut the bone accurately during the operation.
The back wall and column were rebuilt with a tantalum implant and a pelvic plate and screws.
Discharge Summary:
He left the hospital with normal phosphorus and FGF23 levels, a pain-free left hip, and no hardware problems.
He was able to hike again and walk on a treadmill without discomfort or difficulty.
Six months later, he had no hip pain, most of his bone pain had gone, and no new fractures.
His phosphorus level stayed normal at 3.4 mg/dL six months after surgery, indicating good bone health.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 2-month-old male infant, was admitted to our pediatric antiretroviral clinic with the complaint of fever, which was occurring every 2 to 3 days. The mother of the patient reported that the fever was associated with nonprojectile vomit containing recently ingested milk formula. Upon examination, the patient was found to have hepatic and splenic enlargement of 4 cm each. A diagnosis of sepsis was made and the patient was treated with intravenous cefuroxime before complete blood count investigation. Fever resolved 2 days after commencing antibiotics and the patient was discharged home on oral cefuroxime.

The patient was re-admitted a week later with the complaint of fever recurring every 2 to 3 days. A diagnosis of malaria was made upon detection of trophozoites of Plasmodium falciparum in the peripheral blood film. The patient was treated with oral quinine and showed a remarkable improvement in his condition, with the intermittent fever resolving by crisis within 24 hours of administration. The packed cell volume of 26% at readmission increased to 32% on the fourth day of quinine therapy. The child remained well and was discharged home two days after.

Follow-up Recommendations:
The patient is advised to continue co-trimoxazole prophylaxis as previously prescribed and follow up with the pediatric antiretroviral clinic for routine monitoring.

Patient Education:
The mother of the patient is advised to be vigilant in reporting signs and symptoms of fever and to consider malaria as a potential diagnosis in the event of persistent fever. She is also advised to continue the patient's medication regimen as prescribed and follow up with the pediatric antiretroviral clinic for routine monitoring.

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted to our hospital due to 1 hour of severe chest pain. The electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation in leads I and AVL. Laboratory results indicated an elevated serum creatine kinase and troponin I. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) was performed, and the culprit was found to be left circumflex artery occlusion with triple vessel disease. Aspiration thrombectomy and percutaneous coronary balloon dilation were successful in achieving coronary reperfusion. The cardiac surgeon recommended completing the CABG surgery after the acute phase of AMI; however, the patient declined surgery due to her advanced age. 

On the 6th day of hospitalization, the patient experienced sudden chest pain, dyspnea, agitation, and profuse sweating. An electrocardiogram did not show ST-segment elevation, but the patient was found to have atrial fibrillation with a heart rate of 140 beats per minute, which was treated with electrical defibrillation. The patient was diagnosed with pericardial tamponade and underwent pericardiocentesis with ultrasound guidance. Continuous drainage of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion stabilized her hemodynamic condition. 

A subsequent echocardiogram revealed an abnormal cardiac chamber adjacent to the lateral wall of the left ventricle with a myocardial defect (11 mm) in the lateral wall. The diagnosis was congestive hemodynamic impairment caused by the rupture of the left ventricle after acute myocardial infarction, followed by acute pericardial tamponade. While the patient was advised to undergo surgery, she opted for conservative treatment with drug regimens that included dual antiplatelet, statin, β-blocker, and diuretics. 

During her 36-month follow-up, there were no significant changes in her condition. The volume of the pesudoaneurysm increased to 65 × 55 mm only during the initial 2 months of follow-up. After 1 year, color Doppler ultrasound revealed that the blood flow within the aneurysm cavity decreased and echoes of the thrombus were observed. Once the thrombus almost filled the aneurysm cavity after 1.5 years, partial blood flow imaging was seen only nearby the defect of the left ventricular, which was confirmed by myocardial contrast echocardiography. Given the dynamic changes in the pseudoaneurysm, conservative treatment was continued. After 2.5 years of onset of AMI, the patient experienced angina and underwent LAD and RCA PCI. Following medication adherence and no significant changes during the follow up for 3 years, dual antiplatelet therapy was discontinued. 

Discharge Diagnosis: Congestive Hemodynamic Impairment, Pseudoaneurysm of the Left Ventricular, Triple Vessel Disease

Disposition: 

The patient was discharged in stable condition with instructions to follow up with cardiology for routine medication monitoring and outpatient procedures as needed. The patient was informed of the importance of medication adherence and regular follow-up visits.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital with severe headache and intermitting nausea. Imaging-studies showed a tumor in the posterior horn of the left lateral ventricle. A first surgical extirpation of the tumor was performed in 2002 at an external hospital. During postoperative reconvalescence, the patient suffered from several conditions including heparin-induced thrombocytopenia II, pulmonary embolism, deep venous thrombosis, and basal ganglion infarction with consecutive right-sided hemiparesis.

Two years after the meningioma extirpation, the patient suffered from recurring headaches, dizziness, and ataxia. A cerebral CT-scan showed hydrocephalus, for which ventriculoperitoneal shunting was performed in 2004. The patient recovered well after the procedure. In 2005, the patient was diagnosed with a hemorrhaged tumor located in the caudal section of the aqueduct and dorsolaterally to the fourth ventricle. The tumor was removed, and the pathological examination revealed a recurrently hemorrhaged cavernoma with regressive transformations.

In 2008, recurrence of the tumor in the posterior horn of the left lateral ventricle was discovered on MRI scans at the same location as the tumor before (2002). Additionally, another tumor located in the quadrigeminal lamina was detected. In 2009, surgical resection of the tumor in the left lateral ventricle was performed. The pathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of a collision tumor consisting of components of a meningioma and a cavernoma.

Postoperative MRI showed no residual tumor, and the tumor in the quadrigeminal lamina seemed to be regressing. No adjuvant treatment was recommended due to the benign characteristics of both tumor entities and the spontaneous regression of the tumor in the quadrigeminal lamina. The patient was discharged in a stable condition.

Diagnoses:
1. Recurrent atypical meningioma WHO II°
2. Recurrently hemorrhaged cavernoma with regressive transformations
3. Hydrocephalus

Procedures:
1. Ventriculoperitoneal shunting
2. Surgical extirpation of tumor, posterior horn of the left lateral ventricle
3. Surgical resection of collision tumor

Condition on Discharge:
The patient was discharged in a stable condition without any evidence of tumor recurrence in the MRI follow-up.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient is advised to attend regular MRI follow-ups to monitor any potential tumor recurrence and report any new symptoms to the healthcare provider immediately.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the Department of Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopaedics with the chief complaint of forwardly positioned upper front teeth. On extra oral examination, it was observed that the patient had symmetric facial appearance, convex profile, and incompetent lips with Class II molar and canine relation bilaterally. An overjet of 7 mm and an overbite of 70% were noted. Cephalometric findings showed a hypodivergent growth pattern, skeletal Class II malocclusion with protruded maxilla and reduced mandibular length. Furthermore, orthopantomogram findings revealed erupting mandibular third molars. Based on the patient's diagnostic parameters and arch discrepancies, fixed orthodontic mechanotherapy with the extraction of all four first premolars was decided.

Treatment:
Maxillary and mandibular dentitions were bonded using slot brackets, and initial alignment was done with progressing 016 NiTi to 019 × 025 NiTi wires. Later, 019 × 025 stainless steel wires were continued for 1 month followed by the extraction of all four first premolars. Miniscrews were placed in the maxillary arch with respect to the maxillary second premolar and the maxillary molar for retraction of maxillary incisors. Concurrently, mandibular buccal segment protraction was performed using Class II elastics. Customized utility arch correction was done with 016 × 022 TMA wire for deep bite correction along with Class II mechanics. Final finishing and detailing were done with settling elastics. The total duration of treatment was 22 months.

Outcome:
The patient's final orthodontic treatment had satisfactory results with ideal overjet and overbite as well as achieving Class I canine and molar relation. The patient showed improvement in smile esthetics and an optimum soft tissue profile. Post-treatment records show that an adequate level of lip competence was achieved.

Follow-up:
The patient's long-term retention was planned to sustain the correction achieved in her orthodontic treatment. A long-term follow-up protocol was prescribed for monitoring of erupted mandibular third molars and maintenance of occlusion stability. The patient was scheduled for periodic evaluations to minimize the chances of relapse.

Her back teeth were in a Class II relationship on both sides, meaning they were too far back.
She had an overjet of 7 mm and an overbite of 70%, which means her upper teeth stuck out too far and her lower teeth were too high.
X-ray measurements showed her jaw grew forward, giving a skeletal Class II pattern with a protruding upper jaw and a short lower jaw.
An orthopantomogram revealed that her lower wisdom teeth were erupting, which means they were coming in.
Based on these findings, the orthodontist decided to use braces to move the teeth and remove all four first premolars.
Treatment:
Brackets were placed on both the upper and lower teeth, and the teeth were aligned using 016 nickel-titanium wire, then 019×025 nickel-titanium wire.
Next, a 019×025 stainless steel wire was used for one month, after which all four first premolars were removed.
Small titanium screws were placed in the upper jaw near the second premolar and the molar to pull the front teeth back.
At the same time, the lower back teeth were pushed forward using rubber bands on the inside of the cheeks.
A special wire was used to correct the bite depth and to maintain the Class II relationship.
Final adjustments were made with settling rubber bands to ensure the teeth fit together properly.
The treatment lasted a total of 22 months, which is about 1.8 years, from start to finish.
Outcome:
The final braces treatment gave the patient an ideal overjet and overbite, and the canine and molar teeth were in a Class I relationship.
Her smile looked better and her gum line was optimal, giving her a more attractive appearance.
After treatment, her lips could close normally, showing good lip competence and preventing tooth exposure.

The plan is to keep the teeth in the new position with long-term retainers to maintain the treatment results.

Admitting Diagnosis: Hepatitis B virus-related liver cirrhosis with portal vein thrombosis and portal systemic encephalopathy.

Hospital Course:
The patient underwent donor liver transplantation and was admitted to the surgical intensive care unit for postoperative care. Medications included aspirin and nafamostat mesilate to prevent thrombosis, prostaglandin E1 to vasodilate the anastomosed vessels, tacrolimus and prednisolone for immunosuppression, and ampicillin/sulbactam, fluconazole, and nystatin for prophylaxis against infection.

On postoperative day 6, the patient showed deteriorated mental status and decreased motor power on both upper extremities (grade III) and lower extremities (grade I). A neurologic examination was performed by a neurologist. Over the next 6 days, the patient experienced seizures with abnormal mouth chewing movements, which were controlled by the administration of antiepileptic drugs (AED). A brain computed tomography (CT) scan on pod 15 showed that the existing intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) had decreased slightly.

Disposition: The patient was discharged two weeks later and demonstrated movement in blinking his eyes and shaking his head. Follow-up brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a 50% decrease in the size of the ICH three months after liver transplantation. 

Diagnosis at discharge: Hepatitis B virus-related liver cirrhosis with portal vein thrombosis, portal systemic encephalopathy, and intracerebral hemorrhage.

Hospital Course Summary:

Admission Date: 
Discharge Date: 

History of Present Illness:
The patient, a 52-year-old man with no significant medical history, presented with a dry cough, recurrent streaky hemoptysis and occasional low grade fever for the last one and half years. The expectoration was mucoid, scanty in amount and there was no postural or seasonal variation. Fever was of low grade (up to 100°F), and irregular, without any definite periodicity. 

Physical Examination:
The patient was well built and well-nourished with no clubbing or peripheral lymphadenopathy. Respiratory system examination was essentially normal except impaired percussion note and diminished vesicular breath sound in the left infraclavicular region. Trachea was central in position. Cardiovascular system (CVS) and Central Nervous System (CNS) and abdominal examinations were unremarkable. 

Diagnostic Evaluation:
Complete blood count and blood biochemistry was normal except anemia (Hb: 10.8 gm %) and high ESR (40 mm/hr). HIV serology was nonreactive, and sputum smear failed to show any AFB on two occasions. Chest X-ray revealed nonhomogenous opacity in left upper zone with upward and forward retraction of oblique fissure, left hilar prominence and raised left hemidiaphragm. CECT thorax showed collapse-consolidation with a few air bronchograms and tiny calcification in the left upper lobe. 

Fiberoptic Bronchoscopy:
The patient underwent fibroptic bronchoscopy, which revealed hyperemic and swollen bronchial mucosa of the left upper lobe with a globular mass, which was partially occluding the left upper lobe opening. Biopsy was taken from the mass, white cheesy material was seen coming out of it, and it was sent for HPE. BAL fluid was also sent for Gram stain and C/S, AFB stain and M. Tuberculosis culture. The BAL fluid failed to show any organism in smear, but the bronchial biopsy showed typical caseating epitheloid granuloma. Postbronchoscopic sputum showed AFB in smear examination. The BAL fluid grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis after three weeks. 

Management:
After review of the investigation reports, the patient was started on Category I ATD (2H 3R3Z3E3/4H3R3) under DOTS along with oral prednisolone. Three months post-treatment, repeat bronchoscopy showed restored patency of the left upper lobe bronchus with stenosis.

Discharge Diagnosis:
Tuberculosis

Disposition:
The patient was discharged in stable condition and instructed regarding TB care, including medication schedule, importance of compliance with therapy, and proper precautions to be taken when coughing and in public settings. Follow-up appointment was scheduled with the primary care physician.

The patient had no further signs of infection at the time of writing.

Diagnosis:
Descending aortic aneurysm

Procedures:
Transcatheter endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR)

Condition at Discharge:
The patient was discharged without serious complications.

The patient was monitored via computed tomography 15 months after TEVAR repair, at which point there was significant regression of the aneurysm. The patient was free from antibiotics at the time of writing.

Admitting Diagnosis: Hypercalcaemic hyperparathyroid crisis 

Hospital Course: 

The patient was admitted to our tertiary referral center from a regional hospital with hypercalcaemic hyperparathyroid crisis. He presented with a two-week history of weakness and lethargy and a one-week history of vomiting, polyuria and polydipsia. He became confused 24 hours prior to his admission and registered 12 on the Glasgow Coma Scale. On examination, he had a left-sided mass in the anterior triangle of his neck measuring 3 × 3 cm. An ultrasonography of his neck showed a 4 × 3 cm large cyst in the left lobe of his thyroid gland. He was normotensive, with a regular pulse of 70 beats/min. 

Initial management included aggressive fluid resuscitation, cardiac monitoring and the administration of intravenous bisphosphonates. A left thyroid lobectomy and left lower parathyroidectomy were performed. Biopsy revealed a 4 cm parathyroid carcinoma within the cyst, which was fully excised. The patient remained intubated and ventilated overnight in the intensive care unit. His metabolic laboratory profile resolved quickly following the surgery. A lower respiratory tract infection delayed his initial recovery. 

The patient was discharged home 24 days after surgery on oral calcium supplementation. He has been followed up for 6 months so far without any complications or disease recurrence. 

Summary of Care: 

The patient was admitted with hypercalcaemic hyperparathyroid crisis and managed with aggressive fluid resuscitation, cardiac monitoring and the administration of intravenous bisphosphonates. Following a left thyroid lobectomy and left lower parathyroidectomy, he was discharged home on oral calcium supplementation and has been followed up for 6 months without any complications or disease recurrence. 

Disposition: Discharged. 

Instructions: 
- Continue taking oral calcium supplementation as directed 
- Follow up with your primary care physician in 2 weeks 
- In case of any emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency department.

Patient Name: [Redacted]

Hospital Course:
A 9-year-old male patient was admitted to our hospital with sudden loss of vision in his left eye for the past 10 days, following an episode of vigorous eye rubbing. On examination, corneal ectasia with Vogt's striae was observed in the right eye along with a superficial corneal scar. The left eye exhibited dense stromal edema along with a central corneal ectasia, indicating acute hydrops. A diagnosis of bilateral keratoconus with left eye acute hydrops was made based on the clinical findings.

Treatment and Procedures:
The patient underwent pneumodesmetopexy with C3F8 in the left eye, with AC paracentesis using a 26-gauge needle under aseptic conditions. Air was first added to completely fill the anterior chamber (AC) and then replaced with 14% of C3F8 to fill two-thirds of the AC. Topical antibiotics and steroids were prescribed, and the patient was advised to remain in a supine position postoperatively.

Outcome:
The patient has been followed up for 12 months, and the corneal edema has completely resolved. The patient currently has a nebular grade corneal scar and the best-corrected visual acuity is 6/9 (with contact lens). Intraocular pressure (IOP) has been normal postoperatively.

Impressions and Plan:
The patient was treated for bilateral keratoconus with left eye acute hydrops through pneumodesmetopexy with C3F8. The patient’s corneal edema completely resolved, and the best-corrected visual acuity has improved with contact lens. The patient has been discharged with long term follow-up recommended.

The patient presented with a history of a slow-growing, painless cyst in the right lateral orbital region, which was evaluated through mechanical ptosis, proptosis, and slight hypotropia. The patient declined surgical removal with boney reconstruction and continued with periodic aspiration. Sclerotherapy was performed after obtaining informed consent and aspirating the fluid multiple times. The first sclerotherapy was performed with 10 mL of 1% lidocaine containing 1:100,000 epinephrine and 10 mL of absolute ethanol was instilled, and the cavity was washed again with 10 mL of saline. Second and third sclerotherapies were performed at intervals of 3 months. After the final sclerotherapy, the cyst had shrunk in size, and no re-expansion was seen during a 1-year follow-up after the last sclerotherapy. The patient complained of visual field disturbance due to redundant skin, and a blepharoplasty was performed concomitant with incisional biopsy of the cyst. Histopathological examination showed that the specimen comprised dermis with well-developed sweat and sebaceous glands, compatible with a dermoid cyst.

Condition at Discharge:
The patient's dermoid cyst was treated successfully with sclerotherapy and incisional biopsy. At the time of discharge, the patient demonstrated no evidence of a recurring cyst.

Follow-Up Plan:
The patient will continue follow-up care with her primary care physician near her home residence and is advised to inquire if any new symptoms arise.

An 8-year-old male child was admitted to our hospital with cardiac failure. The patient had a history of TOF repair and left pulmonary arterioplasty two years ago at the referring hospital. Echocardiogram conducted during admission showed the presence of a large residual muscular outlet ventricular septal defect (VSD) likely following VSD patch dehiscence. Cardiac catheterization was performed for further evaluation which confirmed the presence of VSD via angiogram. The right ventricular pressure was high at systole, and angiogram in the main pulmonary artery showed dilated right pulmonary artery while the left pulmonary artery (LPA) was completely occluded.

Intervention:

Radio-frequency (RF) energy was applied to the blind-ending channel of the proximal LPA to recanalize the occluded artery. A 2mm × 10mm coronary balloon was inflated at the atretic segment of LPA and a 6mm × 20mm cutting balloon was used to perform balloon dilatation. A 10mm × 17mm stent was used to address the atretic segment, which was further dilated using an 8mm×40mm Powerflex PTA balloon. The patient was discharged 3 days after the procedure with aspirin at 5mg/kg.

Follow-up:

The patient was readmitted 4 weeks after the procedure for the revision of the VSD patch. Repeat cardiac catheterization conducted three months later shows that the LPA stent is patent and the LPA had increased in size with improved left lung arborization. A localized segment of the left lower lobe artery was stenosed (2.4mm), which was subsequently redilated using an 8mm × 20mm peripheral Flextome cutting balloon.

Outcome:

A Formula 418 Expandable stent was implanted to the stenotic segment distal to the first stent with satisfactory results. The LPA and distal pulmonary arterial tree appear healthy and are of satisfactory size for future growth. Repeat cardiac catheterization conducted four months after the initial intervention showed a reduction of the right ventricular pressure of 41 end-diastolic pressure 8 mmHg (simultaneous aortic pressure: 91/50 mmHg, mean: 66 mmHg).

Conclusion:

The patient was discharged in stable condition with aspirin therapy. The guardian of the patient was instructed to follow-up with their local pediatric cardiologist for routine monitoring and care.

Hospital Course:

Patient is a 77-year-old female who presented with right L2-3 radiculopathy that was refractory to maximum medical management. This was secondary to foraminal compression at L2-3 and L3-4 due to degenerative disc disease, levoscoliosis, as well as grade 1 spondylolisthesis at both levels.

Treatment:

Given the patient’s prior history of posterior decompressive laminectomy, it was felt that the best approach would be a minimally invasive lateral approach to obtain indirect decompression of the foramina as well as correct her spinal deformity. This will achieve the goals of decompression and fusion as well as deformity correction while avoiding the risk of operating through scar tissue. A retroperitoneal transpsoas approach was used to expose the disc spaces from the patient’s left side.

Complete discectomy was performed with the release of the contralateral annulus fibrosis followed by the interbody fusion. A lordotic PEEK graft was used at each level, 50 mm length x 18 mm width x 9 mm height, packed with demineralized bone matrix (DBM).

Outcome:

Postoperative anteroposterior and lateral x-ray imaging confirmed good position of interbody grafts, correction of scoliosis as well as spondylolisthesis, and restoration of disc height achieving satisfactory foraminal indirect decompression. A routine postoperative x-ray at three months demonstrated lateral cage migration on the left side at the L2-3 level with evidence of arthrodesis in the disc space.

The patient remained asymptomatic and follow-up imaging at one year demonstrated completed fusion without further migration of the interbody graft at L2-3.

Conclusion:

Informed patient consent was obtained prior to treatment and with the patient’s permission, we report on this case of successful minimally invasive lateral approach to obtain indirect decompression of the foramina as well as correct spinal deformity. The patient had significant improvement and remained asymptomatic.

The patient underwent emergent pericardial drainage, and the fluid analysis revealed it as a hemorrhagic pericardial effusion. The septic screen was negative, and vasculitis screening with ANA and ANCA was also negative. A PET CT scan did not detect any malignant focus. An MRI scan of the heart showed basal septal mid-wall myocardial enhancement of non-ischemic pattern, likely due to myocarditis or cardiomyopathy.

Diagnosis:
After ruling out secondary causes of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion, such as malignancy, autoimmune diseases, and TB, our patient was labeled as idiopathic myocarditis leading to chronic pericardial effusion based on MRI scan of the heart.

Management:
The patient's headache was relieved after pericardiocentesis, and his blood pressure stabilized after resuming his home antihypertensive medications. The patient was observed in the hospital for ten days with regular echocardiogram studies. He was asymptomatic and discharged with regular follow-up in the cardiology clinic. The cardiologist outpatient follow-ups with repeated echocardiogram studies for a further five months did not show any fluid reaccumulation. The patient was followed for one year after discharge where he remained clinically stable.

Idiopathic myocarditis leading to chronic pericardial effusion.

Follow-up:
The patient will have regular follow-up in the cardiology clinic to monitor the progress of the patient's condition.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 39-year-old woman diagnosed with plasmablastic IgA lambda multiple myeloma

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to our facility in January 2011 with a diagnosis of plasmablastic IgA lambda multiple myeloma, stage III (International Staging System). She underwent four cycles of PAD chemotherapy (bortezomib, adriamycin, and dexamethasone) and zoledronic acid before receiving an autologous peripheral blood stem cell transplant, conditioned with melphalan (200 mg/m2), in August 2011. The patient experienced a symptomatic relapse with a T7 vertebral collapse in March 2013, after which treatment with lenalidomide and dexamethasone was initiated. Due to a loss of response after four cycles of treatment, the patient received VCD chemotherapy (bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone), achieving a second complete remission. In December 2013, a fully matched sibling hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, after reduced-intensity conditioning regimen, was performed to consolidate the excellent response. The patient experienced another bone marrow relapse, along with a plasmacytoma of tibia in April 2014, following which she was retreated with VCD. This regimen was stopped after two cycles of treatment due to bortezomib-related peripheral neuropathy. The patient was then placed on VBCMP/VBAD chemotherapy (vincristine, carmustine, cyclophosphamide, melphalan, prednisone/vincristine, carmustine, doxorubicin, and high-dose dexamethasone), achieving a third complete remission.

In April 2015, the patient presented with pericardial effusion and echocardiographic signs of cardiac tamponade, which were resolved through pericardiocentesis. In May 2015, the patient presented with massive left-side pleural effusion. Two thoracocentesis revealed plasmablastic cells. Despite this EMM relapse, multiple myeloma was not detected in blood, urine, or bone marrow. The patient was then started on carfilzomib plus dexamethasone, which resulted in a sudden improvement in her general condition and was discharged without pleural effusion.

Follow-Up Recommendations:

The patient is currently receiving the 18th cycle of treatment and remains in complete remission 19 months after the EMM was detected. Further follow-up appointments will be scheduled to monitor the patient's progress.

The patient was prescribed acetazolamide to be taken 500 milligrams every six hours.
